12805-the-boy-allies-in-the-balkan-campa:
Clair W. Hayes sent his Boy Allies, Hal Paine and Chester Crawford, to the Balkans in this 1916 war adventure. The story opens in the air at dawn, with a sick passenger named Stubbs begging to get back to earth, while Hal guides their military aeroplane. Battles, escapes, and a struggle to save a nation follow.

Hand-to-hand fights, including a wrestling bout where Nicolas drops Ivan by the legs, give the action its punch. The boys move between armies, spies, and mountain roads in the series' brisk style. Young readers of the war years got here a stirring, if simple, Balkan tale.
20549-historic-tales-the-romance-of-real:
Charles Morris wrote his Historic Tales series to bring the past alive as story, and this ninth volume, published in 1908, covers Scandinavia. It retells the history and legends of Sweden, Norway, and Denmark. Kings, vikings, and heroes fill its pages.

One tale reaches back to the days of the early legends. Many centuries ago, the book says, there reigned over Uppsala in Sweden a king named Erik. He had no son and only one daughter, but this girl was worth a dozen sons and daughters of other men. Morris aimed such tales at family reading, history with the blood still in it.
21841-the-saddle-boys-in-the-grand-canyo:
Frank Haywood lifts his glasses on a canyon trail in this Saddle Boys adventure by Captain James Carson, published in 1913. His friend Bob Archer, a Kentucky lad, rides beside him. A wolf pack's work opens the tale, and a floating bottle starts the mystery. Soon the boys are bound for the Grand Canyon itself, with their horse Buckskin standing guard along the way.

A hermit in a cave waits at the heart of the canyon country. Chapters bring a listener under a window, a stand for the law, and a Moqui caught napping. Carson wrote the series for boys who loved the range. It is western series fiction at full gallop: scenery, danger, and two steady lads.
26081-fighting-the-traffic-in-young-girl:
Ernest A. Bell's 1910 exposé attacks the traffic in young girls, which he calls the greatest crime in the world's history. Chapters trace the trade from Babylon, Greece, and Rome to the modern city, then set out how procurers coax girls away and deliver them to dive-keepers. Ice cream parlors and fruit stores appear as common first traps.

Bell prints poems, pictures, and an introduction by Edwin W. Sims, and he charges that police often return escaped girls to the dives or send them to prison instead of helping them. The book ends as a call to action, urging readers and officials to break the trade and protect girls before they are drawn in.
32746-the-revival-of-irish-literature-ad:
Sir Charles Gavan Duffy, George Sigerson, and Douglas Hyde address the Irish Literary Society in London in this 1894 volume. Duffy speaks in July 1892 and June 1893 on what Irishmen may do for Irish literature and on books for the Irish people. Sigerson traces the origin and setting of that literature, and Hyde urges the de-Anglicising of Ireland.

Duffy recalls a fruitful age before the famine of 1846, when young writers dug up buried history and sang songs of valor and hope. Famine, prison, and exile broke their work, yet it fed two generations. The speakers call for Irish books, Irish speech, and a place for Irish in public exams.
britannica-1911-carus-karl-gustav:
Karl Gustav Carus (1789–1869) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a German physiologist and psychologist who was also known as an art critic and landscape painter. Born and educated at Leipzig, he turned to medicine in 1811 and chose comparative anatomy as his lecture subject, a field no one had taught at Leipzig before. He directed a military hospital in the war of 1813 and became professor at the new medical college in Dresden in 1814.

Carus spent the rest of his life in Dresden, becoming royal physician in 1827 and privy councillor in 1862. In philosophy he followed Schelling, and that spirit runs through his work. He treated inherited tendency as proof that the cell holds a kind of psychic life. His chief books include the outlines of comparative anatomy and physiology of 1828 and Psyche, on the history of the soul's development, in 1846.
britannica-1911-cohn-gustav:
Gustav Cohn (born 1840) was a German economist born at Marienwerder in West Prussia on 12 December 1840. He studied at Berlin and Jena. In 1869 he took a post at the polytechnic in Riga. In 1875 he was chosen as professor at the polytechnic at Zürich. A study trip to England in 1873 shaped a key book.

That book treated English railway policy and appeared in 1874 and 1875. In 1884 Cohn became professor of political science at Göttingen. His best known works fill the rest of the entry. They include a system of political economy from 1885 and a work on finance from 1889. Studies in economics came in 1886. A history and politics of transport followed in 1900. The entry is a plain record of posts and books.
britannica-1911-freytag-gustav:
Gustav Freytag (1816-1895), German novelist, was born at Kreuzburg in Silesia on 13 July 1816. He studied philology at Breslau and Berlin, taught at Breslau from 1839, and turned to the stage, winning a lasting place with the comedy Die Journalisten in 1853. From 1848 he co-edited Die Grenzboten, which became the leading voice of German and Austrian liberalism.

His novel Soll und Haben of 1855 was translated into nearly every European language and made his name abroad, praising the German middle class as the soundest part of the nation. Die verlorene Handschrift followed in 1864, and his five-volume Bilder aus der deutschen Vergangenheit pictured German life across the ages. From 1872 he built Die Ahnen, a chain of historical novels following one family to modern times. He rode with the Prussian crown prince staff in 1870 and died at Wiesbaden in April 1895.
britannica-1911-fulleborn-georg-gustav:
Fulleborn, Georg Gustav (1769–1803), a German author and scholar, was born at Glogau on the 2nd of March 1769 and died at Breslau on the 6th of February 1803. He studied at Halle and became professor of classics and philosophy at the Elisabeth gymnasium in Breslau. His Beiträge zur Geschichte der Philosophie helped make the systems of the ancient philosophers known to German readers.

He also wrote an Encyclopaedia philologica in 1798 and a manual on rhetoric. Under the pen name Edelwald Justus he published popular tales drawn from Silesian folk stories, alongside a drama and lighter writings.
britannica-1911-hotho-heinrich-gustav:
Heinrich Gustav Hotho (1802–1873) was a German historian of art, born at Berlin in 1802. Measles left him blind for two years in boyhood, but he recovered his sight and studied so hard that he took his degree at Berlin in 1826. A year of travel through Paris, London and the Low Countries fixed his calling. He came home delighted with the art he had seen.

Hotho passed as docent in aesthetics and art history, and in 1829 became professor at Berlin university. In 1833 Waagen took him as assistant in the Prussian capital's museum. In 1858 he rose to direct its print-room. His time split between writing and official duties for a long, busy life. His ambition was always to master the schools of Germany and the Netherlands, and most of what he published kept to those fields. He died in his native city on Christmas day 1873.
doe-osti-3000129-low-temperature-cyclic-:
Qizhen Li of Washington State University wrote this final report for award DE-SC0016333 on how the lightest structural metal tires. Magnesium weighs less than any rival structural metal, so car and aircraft parts made from it save fuel. Yet magnesium's hexagonal crystal packing gives it unusual slip and twinning behaviour, and parts under repeated loading can fail by fatigue in ways designers still cannot fully predict, especially in the cold.

The project bent ultrafine-grained pure magnesium back and forth at low temperatures and watched the damage build. Processing routes that refine the grain structure were explored alongside, to see how they shift strength and fatigue life. Results appeared in journal articles and talks at TMS, MRS and plasticity conferences. The work serves both alloy designers and the wider public case for magnesium in passenger vehicles: lighter cars, better fuel economy, lower emissions.
doe-osti-3816579-local-air-quality-impac: Waynesville got diesel-peak-shaved, and this DOE text covers North Carolina air quality. The pages detail the local findings. The environmental folks get their data. The unit was generator. The data were environmental. The Carolina were North. The diesel were peak-shaving.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KairysDavidRudo: Harold Weisberg wrote to David Kairys and David Rudovsky on May 1, 1976. Both men were lawyers known for civil liberties work, the kind of counsel a records litigant would write to. The archive's entry names the parties and the date but gives nothing of the letter's substance. It stands as a single dated letter in Weisberg's legal correspondence.
nasa-tm-19640017334-on-the-structure-of-: Two Goddard Space Flight Center authors wrote this February 1964 paper on the structure of a collision-free wave in a plasma. The wave runs across a magnetic field, as the title states. Plasma is hot, charged gas, and collision-free waves cross it without particles striking each other. The hosted sample preserves only the report's title page, with no readable abstract or body text, so its analysis cannot be described from the sample itself.
nasa-tm-19700026442-an-empirical-techniq:
The Mathematical Physics Branch at the Manned Spacecraft Center in Houston issued this internal note on June 2, 1969. It gives a practical technique for computing navigation covariance matrices. Such matrices state how unsure a spacecraft's known position is, and planners needed honest figures for lunar orbit flights after Apollo 8.

The technique rests on real postflight tracking work from Apollo 8 and Lunar Orbiter III. Those flights showed the Moon's gravity field was known less well than planners had assumed. Measured errors in chosen orbit values feed the method, which then produces the expected navigation accuracy. Applied to Missions F and G, it modeled the slow growth of down-track position errors well.
the-boy-allies-in-the-balkan-campaign-or:
Clair W. Hayes wrote The Boy Allies in the Balkan Campaign, or The Struggle to Save a Nation, dated 1916. The first chapter is called In the Air. It opens in a war aeroplane at dawn, high and cold. Hal Paine flies the craft, with three riders behind him.

One of those riders, Mr. Stubbs, sits curled in a ball and groans at times. When Hal asks how he feels, Stubbs says he is sick. He asks how long it will be till they land, so he may die in peace. Hal laughs and tells him he will not die. Chester Crawford, Hal's close friend, asks where they are. Hal, eyes fixed ahead, says they are somewhere over Central Austria. The first light grows in the east as they fly on.
